#3918. Guide: GTA 6: Tenebrae Lux Walkthrough & Puzzle Solutions

Early on in GTA 6, you'll gain access to the JoySystem, a game console with a handful of games you can play. One of those is Tenebrae Lux, a black and white, first-person puzzle game. In this GTA 6 guide, we have a Tenebrae Lux walkthrough, guiding you through the puzzles to reach the ending.

Tenebrae Lux features randomised elements in some of its puzzles, so your experience may vary from what you see in our images and videos.

On this page: GTA 6: Tenebrae Lux Walkthrough & Puzzle Solutions

Below is our walkthrough of Tenebrae Lux, revealing puzzle solutions and where to find notes.

There are 11 notes to collect in total, but the last two require you to collect the previous nine.

In a single playthrough of Tenebrae Lux, you can find those 9 notes hidden in 17 possible locations. Collecting these 9 notes will then allow you to find the 10th and 11th notes.

After waking up on the island, you must solve at least three grid-based puzzles located on the beach, though there are five to find in total — two of which are necessary if you're looking for every note.

Awaken on the beach and make your way to the shelter on the horizon, as pictured:

Go inside the shelter and head for the wooden boxes directly opposite the entrance:

On the table you'll find Note Location #1, as pictured:

Immediately next to Note Location #1 is a board you can interact with. This is Board Puzzle #1.

As is the case with all the other Board Puzzles, Board Puzzle #1 is randomly selected from a batch of puzzles; you won't always be presented with the same one.

To solve the puzzle, follow the steps in the below videos depending on which puzzle you have in front of you:

In the same area as Board Puzzle #1, you'll find Board Puzzle #2 just to the right of the entrance as you enter. For context, the location is pictured:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving the first two Board Puzzles, you should make your way to the next shack along. First, though, check between them to find an upturned boat on the beach:

This is Note Location #2, where you'll find the note leaning against the boat:

After checking Note Location #2, go inside the shack:

On the right-hand side are some hooks; this is Note Location #3, where you may find a note hanging with some rope and a set of scales:

After checking Note Location #2, enter the shelter to the right. This is what it looks like:

Go inside through the front entrance, as shown:

Head towards the wooden crate at the back-right part of the building:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving Board Puzzle #3, turn around and leave the shack through the door ahead:

Turn right and inspect the railing; this is Note Location #4, where you may find a note on the railing:

After checking Note Location #4, go around to the front of the shack, where you entered the first time:

To the right of the entrance are a couple of crates; this is Note Location #5, where you may find a note resting against the crates:

After solving Board Puzzle #3, exit the shelter and go left along the coast (it's quite a walk):

You will pass a small dock with a door on it to your left, ignore it and continue forward:

Here you'll find Board Puzzle #4 next to a shipping container:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After solving Board Puzzle #4, the shipping container directly next to it will unlock:

Inside is Note Location #6 , with the note leaning against the back:

After collecting the note at Note Location #4, walk all the way back where you came from, then go up to the shack on the raised area:

Go around to the back of the shack to find Board Puzzle #5:

Here are the possible solutions we've found so far:

After completing Board Puzzle #5, turn to your left and go inside the shack:

On the right-hand side is a small table, where you'll find Note Location #7:

After checking Note Location #7, exit the shack and look across the island to find a door in the distance with three lights above it:

Inside is Note Location #8, where there are several crates in which the note may appear:

After checking Note Location #6, go through the door ahead and up the stairs:

You'll come to a room with several things you must pay attention to in order to solve this next puzzle. You'll need to make some notes!

The goal is to input the correct string of numbers into the telephone on the back wall. However, there is no defined phone number for you to use; it is a randomised solution.

To learn the phone number, you must pass through several incarnations of the same room to discover differences in the environment, one by one.

Upon first entering the room, you'll see the text "DEVELOPED USING ZUCHWORKS ENGINE" followed by a Greek letter:

It could be any of the following letters, and each corresponds to a numerical value which you must make a note of:

From the left-hand side and moving clockwise around the room, you may find the following things to inspect:

Vinyl records: Make a note of the price and the RPM values. Add the digits together, e.g. if the price is 50 cents, 5+0=0. Same goes for the RPM:

Lamp: When you enter the room, it will flash a morse code message. Decipher it using the chart located on the right of the console

Wall clock: Make a note of the time, and work out the clockwise angle from the hour to the minute hand. Add the digits of the angle together for the appropriate number (e.g. 2 o'clock, angle 300°, 3+0+0=3):

Calendar: The dates 6th and 31st are circled. More on the calendar later:

Phone ringing: When you enter the room, the phone will ring a certain number of times — note down how many

Framed picture: Make a note of how many figures you can see in the picture:

Emergency Protocols: Make a note of the number of the document. It may be redacted:

Cassette tape: Make a note of the date stated when you play the tape recorder:

Wall picture: The picture shows Roman numerals depicted by pillars — note the number

Once you've noted all of the above, proceed through the door next to the phone and up the stairs. You will find yourself in a new iteration of the same room.

The idea now is to inspect everything again, including the onscreen text with the Roman letter, to search for an anomaly. When you find a number that is different from your notes from the original room, note it down.

For example: In the original room, the framed picture showed 3 people, but in the next room, the picture shows 4 people. Note down '4'.

Observe the calendar; it will now have many dates scratched out:

The first date that's clear after the 6th October correlates with the anomaly you have discovered.

So, make a note of your anomaly and the date, then go through the door again, and repeat until you have found anomalies against the following dates:

If done correctly, you should now have a six-digit number to punch into the phone. In the order of the dates, enter the number followed by '#' to solve the puzzle:

While you're working on the Bunker Puzzle, check the crate on the left-hand side of the room:

This is Note Location #9, where you may find a note inside the crate:

After checking Note Location #9, look on the other side of the room to see a valve on the wall:

This is Note Location #10, where you may find a note just behind the valve:

After completing the Bunker's puzzle, go through the door by the phone one last time and you'll emerge in a new room:

This is Note Location #11, where you may find a note on top of one of the flat carts:

After checking Note Location #11, head outside to the right:

After the first set, look left to find this note, as pictured:

After checking Note Location #12, continue towards some ruins:

On the right, there is a post with a light next to it — this is Note Location #13, where you may find a note atop the post:

After checking Note Location #13, go around to the right-hand side of the ruins:

On the right-hand side is an open crate; this is Note Location #14, where you may find a note inside the crate:

After checking Note Location #14, walk through the ruins to the back, where you can see a pulley system:

There is a closed crate next to it; this is Note Location #15, where a note may appear on the crate:

After checking Note Location #15, return to the front of the ruins and you'll see a plaque with a poem on it (yours may be different to the one pictured):

The poem contains particular words in each line that correspond to the objects you will find in the ruins. The exact locations of these objects are randomised.

Your goal in this puzzle is to cross the bridge towards the lighthouse, walking across glowing symbols in the correct order:

As mentioned, aspects of this puzzle are random, so there is no definite solution.

To discover the correct path across the bridge, you must locate each of the following items, then cross-reference them with your poem to decipher the right order of the symbols.

Brazier (Related poem words: Furnace, Scorch, Heat, Fire, Flames, Fiery):

Fountain (Related poem words: Water, Drink, River, Lakes, Wetlands, Swamps):

Moon Sculpture (Related poem words: Moon, Moonshine, Lunar, Evening, Night, Sleep):

Sundial (Related poem words: Sun, Sunlight, Solar, Sunrise):

Tree (Related poem words: Forest, Woods, Rest):

Trophy (Related poem words: Gold, Riches, Trove, Treasure, Prize):

Vase (Related poem words: Earth, Soil, Ground, Mound):

When you find one of these objects, you must then enter the ruins and observe the object through an opposite archway; the symbol at the top of the arch corresponds to that object. For example:

To recap, you need to do three things to get the answer to cross the bridge:

Once you have this all lined up, approach the bridge and cross the correct symbols in the correct order:

After successfully crossing the bridge (or before you cross it), go back across it towards the ruins, where you just came from:

Find the Brazier in the ruins and walk into it. The character will talk about the tattoo on his hand if you've done it right:

Now go across the bridge again and approach the small hut to the right. It will only unlock if you do the above steps first:

Go inside and you'll find this note on a chair:

After getting the note from Note Location #16, follow the path up to the lighthouse:

Go up the steps on the left side of the lighthouse:

At the top, look right to find this note on the postbox:

As soon as you have collected a total of 9 notes, make your way back to the bunker's phone room. To the left of the console is another door that's now unlocked:

Go inside, and go to the person on the bed:

Beneath him you can observe another note, depicting various phases of the moon:

These moon symbols also appear on the calendar in the phone room, so go back out and check it:

You need to find the dates that match the symbols on the note to create a string of numbers. If the dates have two digits, add them together to make one.

The sequence of symbols and where they appear on the calendar are randomised, so your solution will be different for each playthrough.

In this example, the solution is 2, 2, 1, 1, 6, 3, followed by #.

When you have your number sequence, go to the phone and enter it:

If you've done it correctly, the man on the bed will be gone and you can pick up the note:

After solving the moon symbols puzzle and collecting your 10th note, stay in the bunker's phone room as you have one more number to dial:

Open Tenebrae Lux's pause menu with Touch Pad and select Notes:

Here, you can look at all 10 of your collected notes. Each of them represents a number, as follows:

Your goal is to create another string of numbers based on the order in which your notes appear in your Notes menu. This is random.

So, using the above images as reference and following their order on the Notes menu, create your number sequence, then dial it into the phone, followed by '#':

If you've done it correctly, a cryptic message will play regarding the final note.

The last, 11th note can now be found on the bridge to the lighthouse — walk back there and search the bridge for the note:

It might appear on the railings or on the pillars at either end of the bridge.

Now that you have collected all 11 notes in Tenebrae Lux, there is one more puzzle waiting for you. Open the Notes menu again and you'll find that the first 10 notes now each have a word in bold somewhere on them:

These words are each associated with a number, based on the Kabbalah Tree of Life (unrelated to the game). Here's how it breaks down:

Using this information, you need to put together another number sequence. For example, if the second note in your Notes menu represents #9, and has the word Victory on it (representing 7), the seventh number in your sequence will be 9.

Once you have your number sequence, you need to dial it into the bunker's phone, so go back there if you're not there already:

If you enter the numbers correctly, you will hear another message. Exit the bunker back down onto the beach, and walk back towards the shipping container:

On the way is a small dock with a door on it — you can now enter the door:

Approach the desk and interact with the computer to begin a speedrunning challenge, in which you must complete Tenebrae Lux within 20 minutes.

You don't have to do all this business with the notes again — just get to the lighthouse and complete its puzzle to finish.

After collecting Note #4, go back down the stairs and in through the door at the base of the lighthouse:

You will be presented with a series of doors:

A man will walk through one of them. You need to walk through the farthest possible door from the one he went through:

This puzzle is also somewhat randomised, but use these examples to help. Again, this is just about using the door that's furthest from the other people:

You'll need to do this a number of times, eventually leading to a final cutscene and the game's first ending:

Tenebrae Lux contains 2 possible endings.

You will get the first ending by just completing the game normally:

The second ending requires much more for you to complete:

To begin playing Tenebrae Lux, you must progress enough to unlock the JoySystem console. This occurs in Chapter 1 during the mission Feng Shui.

Once the mission is complete, you will be able to use the JoySystem at any time and begin playing Tenebrae Lux.

Note: During Chapter 2, you will temporarily lose access to the JoySystem, but it will become available again once you start Chapter 3. From there, you will be able to play with no further interruptions.

#3917. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

#3916. Quantum Break Developer Responds To Sequel Demand For The 2016 Xbox Exclusive

"We love the amount of love for the game"

It's been 10 years since Quantum Break made its debut as an Xbox console exclusive in 2016, and Xbox fans have often considered it somewhat of an underated cult classic from the developer behind the likes of Control and Alan Wake.

So, could we get a sequel?! Remedy Entertainment's X account has been talking about this over the last 24 hours, highlighting that the team love how much passion fans still have for the IP, but that the decision is in Xbox's hands.

In other words, it's down to Asha Sharma and her group at Xbox HQ.

Now, to be honest, we don't reckon it's a likely bet. The original Quantum Break was a really cool exclusive for Xbox to have 10 years ago, but it seems like the new Xbox CEO is more interested in focusing on big franchises like Gears, Halo, Fallout and The Elder Scrolls rather than dipping back into something from a difficult period in Xbox's history.

That's not to say it couldn't happen though, and in some ways you'd think it'd be an easy win for Xbox to cater to nostalgia and remind everyone how much they enjoyed the original Quantum Break. Remedy has made sequels to Alan Wake and Control in recent times as well, so they'd surely be up for revisiting QB if given the opportunity.

What do you think, should Xbox greenlight a new Quantum Break game? Let us know in the poll and comments below.

#3915. Star Wars Galactic Racer will get local split-screen multiplayer in early 2027 with new 'Free Play' mode, finally letting racers yell at one another in a tangible space

Split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

This new mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an issue for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming update, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

#3914. The Reason Behind Pokémon's Mysterious Social Media Countdown Has Been Revealed

A few weeks ago, we caught wind of a mysterious countdown taking place on The Pokémon Company's official social media accounts, marking the hours remaining until 30th November at 2pm UTC. We wondered whether it was all for a surprise eShop drop, a Pokémon Presents or a new Winds & Waves trailer, but it looks like it might all be for something much more disappointing.

As pointed out by Serebii, several of the official Pokémon game social media accounts have begun promoting an upcoming Pokémon music video for a track called 'Evergreen', which will drop on YouTube at, you guessed it, 2pm UTC on 30th November.

It could be that this track is part of something bigger — a Presents segment, or maybe some Gen 10 news — but there's a big part of us now that thinks the countdown was focused on this alone which... we should have tempered our expectations for, to be honest.

Serebii Update: A special Pokémon Music Video called Evergreen will release on November 30th at 14:00 UTC The Pokémon Champions, Pokémon TCG Pocket, Pokémon Center and Pokémon Masters EX accounts are all promoting it www.serebii.net

The official Pokémon X account even shared a trailer for the music video, and attached another of the countdown images in the replies thread, noting that there were 151 hours to go. So yes, it certainly looks like this is what all the mystery was about.

*Sigh* We'll pop our tinfoil hats away for now, then...

Original Story: The Pokémon Company is no stranger to a little over-hyping every now and then, but its latest bit of marketing has us seriously thinking that there is a big announcement in the pipeline.

You see, TPC is counting down to... something. As brought to our attention by Serebii's Joe Merrick, the company has been sharing images on social media of its 30th anniversary icons, with a number underneath. Interestingly, these numbers decrease by the number of hours that have passed between each post — 1,025 on 18th October, 843 on 26th, 676 today.

Keeping the countdown going, this means that we'll hit zero on 30th November at 2pm UTC (thanks for doing the maths there, Joe!). The latest post even came with a full message under the logo, roughly translating to "Continue with Pokémon".

Confirmation. We have a third data point 676 hours from now is 14:00 UTC on November 30th 2026. As I predicted, they are counting down to then. What will arrive at that point, it remains a mystery.

Hmm. The big question is, what's this all about? 2pm UTC sure feels like the right time for a big announcement (it's when most eyes, worldwide, will be on it), and we can't imagine that TPC would put this much planning into something inconsequential.

What is it, then? Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire were rumoured to be coming to NSO last month, could it be that? Is it time we got another look at Winds and Waves, perhaps with a firm release date attached? Is there another full Pokémon Presents around the corner? Only time will tell, but it sure is an exciting prospect.

We'll be keeping an eye on the countdown throughout November and will let you know when any major news comes out of it.

#3913. Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

The difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

From a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

It makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make new, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

#3912. Unity launches new Fellowship program, offering a "no recoup" $50,000 grant to indie developers planning to launch their game in the next 12 months

Unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that plan release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the company has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental issues.

Unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

The grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

#3911. GTA 6 Comparison Reveals Two Advantages Of Xbox Series X Over PS5

The good folks over at Digital Foundry are still busy analysing all things to do with GTA 6's launch last week, and their latest comparison takes a look at all four console versions alongside each other - Series X, S, PS5 and PS5 Pro.

They also go on to rank the versions in order, and perhaps surprisingly, Xbox Series X comes out on top versus the standard PS5. Two reasons are given for this, which are that the Xbox version supports 120Hz VRR to smooth out the dips in frame rate, and that the PS5 sometimes "suffers substantially more frequent frame-rate drops than Series X".

"Although both target 30fps and maintain it during typical gameplay, heavy vehicle traversal and intense airport crowd sequences cause frame-rates to drop into the mid to upper 20s. PS5 suffers substantially more frequent frame-rate drops than Series X, which is compounded by the fact that the Xbox machine also benefits from 120Hz VRR support to smooth out minor dips. Ultimately, Series X is meaningfully better off."

Visually, there are said to be no real differences between the Xbox Series X and PS5 versions, although the Series X version does have "slightly more pronounced heat haze effects in one opening shot".

All of this is obviously beaten by the PS5 Pro though, which is said to "deliver the definitive console GTA 6 experience by leveraging its larger GPU, accelerated machine learning hardware and enhanced ray tracing features".

"Overall, the PS5 Pro leads the rankings with its superior visual detail and rock-solid 30fps target, followed by the Xbox Series X - which edges out the standard PS5 through better performance stability. The Xbox Series S sits at the bottom due to visual trade-offs, unstable frame-rates and audio glitches."

It's fair to say we never expected the Xbox Series X version to fare better than the PS5 version in this case, especially considering all the "plays best on PS5" marketing that surrounded GTA 6 prior to release.

Of course, Digital Foundry seeks out the most minute of details when it comes to technical analysis, and the differences between the Xbox Series X and standard PS5 versions aren't going to be major enough to suggest one version is far better than another. It's just interesting that they've ended up ranking the Series X higher in this instance.

Let us hear your thoughts in the comments, but please do keep it respectful! We enjoy the PS5 as well, and know plenty of people who are loving the game on that system. All the same, this is a fascinating analysis and a bonus for Xbox.

#3910. Can GTA 6 make $2 billion in its opening weekend? One industry analyst has run the numbers, and seems to think so

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the company's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

We also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

"That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow."

But it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play."

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

#3909. GTA 6 Officially the 'Biggest Launch in PlayStation History' with Over 39 Million Players

Highest number of concurrent players ever on PlayStation

Sony has shared a selection of staggering statistics relating to the launch of GTA 6 on PS5.

From launch on 19th November through to the end of the title's opening weekend, Sony recorded over 39 million unique players.

The game set a new record on PlayStation for the highest number of concurrent players on any game.

PS5 players have logged 683 million hours of GTA 6 playtime, and on average, every owner on PlayStation has played it for 17.4 hours.

Outside of the console's launch and Christmas holidays, the launch of GTA 6 resulted in "the largest number of newly connected PS5 consoles on a single day". GTA 6 was the first game played on 70% of those new PS5 systems.

#3908. "Games are best made by people": The IWGB and other European unions publish joint manifesto calling on workers, employers and consumers to reject genAI

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is currently harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people."

The manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture."

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the company code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games."

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable."

#3907. Ever wanted to play a multiplayer version of Cyberpunk 2077 with your friends? Well, thanks to a mod now in beta, you can

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers."

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

If you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later announced that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

This isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a new mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

#3906. I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that big a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

Sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

The latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

#3905. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

#3904. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

GTA 6 has been updated to support PS Plus Premium cloud streaming directly to the PS5 and PS Portal.

To be crystal clear about this: the game has not been added to the PS Plus Premium catalogue and you will still need to own it.

However, assuming you’ve purchased the game – and millions of you have – then you’ll now be able to stream it directly from Sony’s servers, assuming you’re a PS Plus Premium member.

There are a number of use cases for this, but the most likely is you’re away from your console and still want to play on your PS Portal. Now you won’t need to rely on Remote Play; you can just stream it directly.

I don't think the "Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!" award counts as a Game of the Year nod

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Valve has opened nominations for the 2026 Steam awards, and for this 10th iteration of the annual event, players are being asked to choose a special winner. The Hall of Fame award will go to one of the ten previous Steam Game of the Year award winners, but there's one problem: Steam didn't have a GOTY category for the first two years of these awards.

That means that the "winners" in 2016 and 2017, Grand Theft Auto 5 and The Witcher 3, were never actually voted on by fans as GOTY-caliber stars. Certainly, both of those games were widely acclaimed when they launched – but The Witcher 3 and the PC version of GTA 5 were both released in 2015, before the Steam awards even existed.

Going back to the first round, the Steam awards offered an array of goofball categories with silly names that nonetheless honored great games. In 2016, GTA 5 did win an award titled "Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!" for games that "melt your face," and in 2017, The Witcher 3 won the "Choices Matter" award for games with a great deal of player agency.

As Valve explains in an FAQ alongside today's nomination announcement, the team used these two awards as a "proxy" to decide on the 2016 and 2017 GOTY picks. But I've gotta ask, why did 2017 not just use "Whoooaaaaaaa, Dude! 2.0," won by The Evil Within 2, for its GOTY? Or the "Even Better Than I Expected" award, explicitly built for games released in 2017 and won by Cuphead?

In fairness, it is fun seeing all-time heavy hitters like GTA 5 and Witcher 3 going up against similar heavyweights like Elden Ring, Baldur's Gate 3, and Hollow Knight: Silksong. And ultimately, none of this matters – as with any set of game awards, it's supposed to simply be an opportunity to celebrate excellent games. But, when did we ever let an award show go by without using it instead as a chance to get mad about the nominees?

#3900. Embracer begin yet another round of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, while they're still midway through development on two Tomb Raider games

Update: Studio confirms eight staff lost their jobs

Update 18/11: Crystal Dynamics have provided the following statement to RPS, confirming it cut eight staff members:

As initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is currently known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

This now marks the studio's fifth round of layoffs since Embracer acquired it in 2022, following cuts in March 2025, August 2025, November 2025, and March this year. This is a drastic amount even considering the current state of the industry, with layoffs seemingly happening several times a week, but unfortunately, this is par for the course for Embracer. Even still, it makes one wonder just how many staff are left at Crystal Dynamics by now. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and Tomb Raider: Catalyst are still in production, so you'd hope that the studio won't be shuttered entirely.

According to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

#3899. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

If you'd like to reminisce a bit before the long-awaited game finally hits, you can check out our favourite Grand Theft Auto pieces Eurogamer's published over the years.

The obvious winner is Resident Evil Village

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The 10th annual Steam awards are upon us, and Valve just opened up voting for nominated games across 14 different categories. The top prize is the Hall of Fame Award for the "#1 game of the past 10 years," which will be chosen from a list of GOTY winners from 2016 to 2025. In order of release year, we have GTA 5, The Witcher 3, PUBG, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Red Dead Redemption 2, Resident Evil Village, Elden Ring, Baldur's Gate 3, Black Myth Wukong, and Hollow Knight Silksong.

Now, depending on how good your memory is, you may or may not be thinking, 'wait a minute, GTA 5 didn't come out in 2016 and The Witcher 3 didn't come out in 2017, so why are they the respective games of the year for those years?' I don't really know, but Valve says in a FAQ it used the 'Whoooaaaaaaa, Dude!" award from 2016 and the "Choices Matter" award from 2017 as proxies for the years Steam didn't give out GOTY awards. GTA 5 and The Witcher 3 won those awards back in 2016 and 2017, so Valve retroactively gave them the GOTY wins for those years and nominated them for the Hall of Fame Award this year.

Anyway, with that little oddity out of the way, it's time to talk about most likely Hall of Fame Award winners. It seems to me that GTA 5, The Witcher 3, Red Dead Redemption 2, Elden Ring, and Baldur's Gate 3 are the frontrunners, but Steam's user base isn't necessarily reflective of the overall gaming community voting for games at, say, the Golden Joystick Awards. I wouldn't be at all surprised to see Metroidvania sickos turn out in droves to vote for Hollow Knight Silksong, and I personally would love to see Resident Evil Village take home the award even if I'm pretty confident that's not going to happen.

Sony misses out on a Game Awards GOTY nomination for the first time in 12 years, with Marvel's Wolverine, Saros, and Marathon failing to continue its record-breaking run

#3897. Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

It's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

It's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

In a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

#3896. Phil Spencer Might Not Be At Xbox Anymore, But He's Still Playing Loads Of Games

Phil Spencer is a legend of the Xbox division, having helped redefine the brand after a disastarous Xbox One launch in 2013, and spearheading such initiatives as Xbox Game Pass, Xbox backwards compatibility, crossplay, and a renewed focus on gaming rather than continuing the push towards "TV, TV, TV" that had proven so controversial.

It's very possible that without his influence, Xbox would have shut its doors over a decade ago.

News Microsoft Considered Pulling The Plug On Xbox Back In 2014

We haven't heard anything from Spencer since he announced his retirement earlier in 2026, but he's still very actively playing games on his Xbox consoles, including some of this year's new releases.

For example, he's racked up 940/1000 gamerscore in Echo Generation 2, 650/1000 in Forza Horizon 6, 585/1000 in Replaced, and he's also been playing the likes of Halo: Campaign Evolved, Gears of War: E-Day, Sopa - Tale of the Stolen Potato, Baldur's Gate 3, Vampire Crawlers and even Sunset Overdrive in recent months.

One of Phil's most beloved qualities as Xbox boss was that he proved himself to be a hardcore gamer, being someone who actively seeks to play games in his spare time. New Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is somewhat the opposite, admitting back in February that she doesn't "pretend to be the best gamer" and that it's ultimately not her goal to be.

Anyway, Phil is busy enjoying his retirement right now, and we wish him all the best from everyone here at Pure Xbox. We unfortunately never got a chance to meet the man ourselves, but always admired his leadership from afar.

Here's hoping he might start hitting the interview circuit and doing what the likes of Peter Moore and Nintendo's Reggie Fils-Aimé have done in the past, as we'd love to see him sticking around the industry in some capacity going forward.

#3895. GTA 6 Is 'Probably the Greatest Artistic Achievement in History', Says Cyberpunk 2 Director

Just about every veteran developer in the industry has been heaping praise on GTA 6 since its release last week, but I'm not sure any of that rampant positivity matches the thoughts of Igor Sarzynski.

Sarzynski is currently the creative director on Cyberpunk 2 (as it's officially known right now), having previously worked on both The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 — two games that are widely considered to be amongst the best that the open world genre has to offer.

In other words, Sarzynski knows what he's talking about when he says GTA 6 is "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history". Now that's praise.

"GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real," he noted on social media.

"Probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, I mean it. Scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle."

"Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled," Sarzynski jokes, suggesting that no one's going to match Rockstar's effort for quite some time. "I'mma go sweep autumn leaves in my backyard now."

GTAVI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real. probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, i mean it. scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle. cyberpunk 2 is cancelled, imma go sweep autumn leaves in my backyard now.

If you've played GTA 6, you can surely understand why every non-Rockstar developer is looking at it and being left in a state of near disbelief. We're not getting another release like it for years and years to come — and just like Red Dead Redemption 2 before it, it's going to become the benchmark for open world games.

Still, there'll come a time when Cyberpunk 2 takes all the headlines — it's just that right now, it's hard to see beyond GTA 6 because it's absolutely bloody everywhere (and with good reason).

"Seriously though I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavour," Sarzynski continues in a follow-up post.

"GTA is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed," he concludes — and that's pretty much a perfect way to put it.

Do you agree with Sarzynski? Just how big of an achievement do you think GTA 6 really is? Have your mind blown in the comments section below.

I'm not trying to put Rockstar down here. Instead of pushing boundaries, as Rockstar have done, most developers are looking for ways to cut corners and get their games out as soon as possible.

Honestly, if a developer such as Larian or CD Red were afforded the time and the money to make the game they really wanted, I am sure we would be equally amazed at what they produce. The truth is, when you look at what Larian and CD Red achieve with a fraction of the budget and half the time, then it makes you realise what technical marvels their games turn out to be.

@Fiendish-Beaver I don’t disagree with your statement in many ways.

However, on the subject of CDPR, with Cyberpunk 2077, every AAA and some even AA studios could absolutely deliver what they have.

They started “work” on Cyberpunk 2077 as far back as 2010-2011 if memory serves.

It was then in and out of development, until about 2016 when it was an all hands on deck approach. Not the start of development, simply at that point many more in the studio working on actively producing a working title.

Then, release came, again, I believe was around 2020. So say at that point 9-10 years of development, with 4 or just under/over years of true entire studio development of some sort.

Yet, they released a game so bad in its basic coding and functionality, that they claimed they weren’t aware of, to then claim they were aware of, then had journalists embargo to not tell of this until launch/very close to launch.

They then offered mass refunds, one of the industries first physical and digital refunds of its kind. Where even I sent them my disc back to their office directly and got a refund.

It then took them up until shall we say about now, maybe being generous a year or so ago to get the game to where most were led to believe it should be and would have been at release.

CDPR conned the public, for financial gain, knowingly, and they squandered hundreds of thousands and likely millions actually on course correcting.

When all they had to do was not release the game until it was finished.

So whilst from what I witness every day in the industry I agree with your points as a whole, we shouldn’t give credit to what CDPR could do with a billion dollars, when the best example of what they did with less was verging on fraudulently selling and advertising a product, pulling it from sale, taking years to “fix” it and then regain consumer confidence.

Many may have forgiven and/or forgotten. They shouldn’t, and I sure won’t.

CDPR have a wonderful vision in their artistry, and I hope they go on to have success upon success. But what R* have achieved is miles beyond what many could achieve even with the money.

There’s numerous engines I’ve used over the years, entire workflows that quite literally can’t physically do what R* have pulled off with their team and technology. It needs really making clear to the laypeople of the world that this isn’t simply more money and talent, this is entirely new ways of approaching how to develop a game and how to use the the resources available.

CDPR literally looked at what they had, made mockups of ideas that were conceptual at best and ran with selling concept art that in some cases they still haven’t accomplished.

I don’t even have a history of playing a lot of R* content. But they have achieved something that money can’t currently buy. That’s the impressive part.

However, as stated, completely agree and disagree but not entirely. 😂 Peace and love on earth etc.

Totally agree, @ButteredCrumpet. I really don't understand where it all went so wrong with CDPR. The game looked immense before it was released, and I bought into it, yet we had all been conned. How on Earth did they think they could get away with it?

I do not expect Cyberpunk 2 to release in the broken state that the first game did. Maybe I've being naïve, but I would like to think they know better than to do that again...

@Fiendish-Beaver Absolutely agree. I believe in them, their talent and their capacity to deliver a game time and time again that is astounding.

Though I didn’t know of anyone on a personal level that worked on the project, it was clear early on something was not quite right with how the studio was handling things internally.

I even remember there being a time where more effort was seemingly being spent on a website, clues for the public and pre-rendered concept art than the game. As at that time they then claimed it was just a pipe dream of sorts.

Yet oddly one they were releasing next and seemingly had not even a mockup of a room or street lamp to speak of.

I personally think they got lost in the vision for a while, knowing as creatives they were onto something new and special. Almost like an artist staring at an oil painting for too long will always find a way to critique and amend it, yet not always objectively improve it.

I have now since gone back to Cyberpunk 2077 and though struggled at first to enjoy it, it has since clicked and I have had a wonderful time with it.

I think the biggest problem in development right now that I am witnessing first had, is simply too many suits trying to predict the next big thing, instead of allowing the next big thing to be naturally found.

Working in lighting and texturing, I can’t create the next big thing, I sort of have to discover it. But of course, that’s where the time and money element do apply. As without it I can’t excuse spending 6 months on a global sabbatical just meandering through the technology and discovering things on a whim.

It’s an odd industry really, it’s a lot like being a pop star, you’re told what to create, the timeline for when it’s expected to be completed, told how much will be charged for it, where and when it will be sold.

Yet you’re never really being told this by people who have much if any experience achieving it, so then you sit back and realise you may not be happy with something, but then my happiness with a texture doesn’t matter.

My happiness with the art I create matters only to the person viewing, yet the person that decides everything I create cares not for my happiness with it.

However, I’m only experiencing what many in and out of creative jobs experience. It’s not like it’s any different being told to move an Amazon parcel onto a conveyor and not wishing to.

I just sometimes wish we could all stop the conveyor and question why some things are being placed on it.

Art shouldn’t be rushed, as the historical examples people have provided on this site show, but then there is little to no industry without reliable performance, predictable results and financial investment.

In an ideal world art and money would never cross paths, but then tell that to Sotheby’s. An entire world of elitist ideals based on paintings by people who died financially bankrupt helping to prop up the wealth of the few.

Hardly what Rembrandt would have really wanted.
