#3834. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

#3833. Slay the Spire 2 is one of this year's best selling games despite only being available on PC, and its players are "obsessed"

One million copies for each month on sale, it seems. Slay the Spire 2, Mega Crit's roguelike deckbuilder, is estimated to have sold 7.9m copies since its release in Steam Early Access in March.

That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.

Slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox. That is notable, as the game is only out on Steam, meaning it has sold enough copies to outpace games on platforms it's not even available on.

We already knew Slay the Spire 2 was one of the year's biggest releases. In its first week on sale, the game sold over 3m copies. It quickly became March's top-selling game on Steam, beating blockbuster competition in Crimson Desert and Resident Evil Requiem. Slay the Spire 2, alongside other indie titles such as Meccha Chameleon, have helped Steam deliver another record year of revenue.

It was such a hit, even, that other indie developers felt it negatively impacted sales of their own games. Mewgenics maker Edmund McMillen recently told Eurogamer "it sucked everybody out". "The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over," McMillen said.

Slay the Spire 2 has been consistently popular with players, too, and that popularity has seemingly continued. Elliott noted the game never fell below 2.5 million active players each month since March.

Slay the Spire 2's loyal following also meant that the recently released beta patch, which added a new character, was enough to bring back millions of players. Despite only being available for players who opt into the beta branch of the game, Slay the Spire 2 more than doubled its daily active users to reach its highest daily player count in six months.

"Simply put: Slay the Spire 2 players are obsessed," wrote Elliott. "And it's not just a niche group of dedicated players, either. The average play time is nearly 84 hours, sure. But zooming out, 1.9 million folks have played for over 100 hours."

Incidentally, nearly 100,000 players bought the game but never played it, which Elliott added could explain the discrepancy between player numbers and copies sold.

Looking ahead, Slay the Spire 2's road to version 1.0 is expected to be long, with several features and gameplay additions still in the works. Then there are the console ports, which have yet to be announced, but are very much expected.

In Eurogamer's Slay the Spire 2 early access review, Bertie Purchese called it "a deceptively familiar sequel" whose confident design and smart new additions build on what made the original work so well.

Here is an incredibly far-off release date you can pencil in (and then probably rub out because it'll be delayed again): the wild and wacky Showa American Story is coming to PS5 on 28th October 2027.

It was originally planned to launch in 2026, so this is a pretty substantial delay to the game, but the "core game content" is now complete, according to the developer.

The next 11 months will be dedicated to "polishing and optimizing the experience so that when you step into Showa American Story, it feels cohesive, responsive, and complete".

Preview Forget the Soulslikes, This Bizarre New PS5 Game Is Channelling Shenmue Instead

For those who don't know, Showa American Story is based on the scenario where "Japan has bought out most of the United States with its strong economic power. A surge of immigration has firmly planted Japanese culture within the American continent. Two cultures are rapidly amalgamated, although conflicts are inevitable, citizens gradually adapt to a life never imagined as time goes by."

This leads to a bizarre adventure, which we got a small taste of at Gamescom earlier this year. You play Chigusa Choko, a female movie star brought back from the dead who sets out on a quest with vibes of Shenmue, Yakuza, and No More Heroes.

What we played was incredibly unfinished and janky, but there was still some promise on show. Let's hope almost a year of polish and further work on the game turns it into a strong experience.

While you're out stealing cars for Moses, the GTA 6 BF Bandito will appear on your list, taking you out to the very rural roads of South Leonard County and the Buckskin Swamp. Here's how to get your hands on the GTA 6 Bandito and get paid.

#3830. Rockstar firings tribunal hears closing statements, with judge promising to deliver a verdict "as quickly as I possibly can" - though it may take a while

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

That's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can."

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

To recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a new company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the big game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

#3829. Clair Obscur's narrative lead has left developer Sandfall Interactive after "wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition"

Last night, it was revealed that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead narrative designer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, won a BAFTA Breakthrough US award for her contribution to the hit 2025 game, which made history after winning 12 Game Award nominations last year. In the aftermath of her win, Svedberg-Yen dropped a pretty big bombshell: she's no longer with the game's developer, Sandfall Interactive.

"No, I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she told Gamesbeat when asked if she's still with the company. "We've parted ways." As to what Svedberg-Yen is doing next, she offered a cryptic answer, including talk of writing "my own projects, my own stories". She also discussed another project she's set her sights on: establishing a fund to help mentor and grow a new generation of video game narrative designers.

"One of the initiatives I want to build is a narrative investment fund to focus on narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers," she explained, noting her background working in finance and how that dovetails nicely with her more recent experience as a narrative lead. "This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face. To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors."

Her motivation for this initiative? Simply, she wants to change how the industry works. "I've discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it's a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations."

"The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help," she added later. "That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don't know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry."

Sandfall Interactive previously said its guiding "North Star" will always be its "own personal taste", and what the team enjoys.She noted that she didn't think the studio would bow to pressure from fans to do more of the same, but instead be guided by what it thinks is best for itself, and for the series. "I've seen too many TV shows and books be swayed trying to please a lot of people, and in the process you end up losing the heart of what's there," she noted.

We know that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is "not the end" of the franchise, and it seems that whatever happens next, it'll have at least a little bit of Svedberg-Yen's creativity instilled in it. I wish her the best for whatever her next step is.

Over the last couple of weeks, some Nvidia users noticed their SSDs were taking a hammering, reporting their driver's log file was being overwritten constantly, sometimes to the tune of 30 GB every hour. Which obviously isn't great for the lifespan of the valuable SSD you've got it installed on.

Given the problem was caused by recent driver updates, rolling back to version 621.01 was the best solution until Nvidia could do something about it. Which they did, releasing a hotfix as version 621.35. It's not available in the GeForce app yet, but you can download it directly from Nvidia's site. Not that you should.

As users on the Nvidia subreddit are reporting, the problem persists. While the hotfix reduces the peak write rate and prevents it for a short while after reboot, it eventually creeps back in. One user reported that overnight the log file was still being rewritten by approximately 4.5 GB every hour.

So yeah, the best solution remains to roll back to version 621.01 and, as always with Nvidia drivers, to hold off on updating to the latest driver until it's been confirmed safe. If this ongoing saga sounds familiar, it's because the same thing happened to AMD's GPU drivers earlier this month. Maybe vibecoding driver updates and then vibecoding fixes for their inevitable bugs isn't the best way of doing things.

#3827. Hour-long Total War: Warhammer 40,000 campaign stream shows off ship battle-less fleet management, makes clear how not ideal getting Space Marine armies killed is

"It would take them decades to recover from that"

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of big ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more quickly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

"Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs said, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

#3826. GTA 6 Performs Better on Xbox Series X Than Base PS5, Despite All of Sony's Marketing

Even though Sony has paid god-only-knows how much money to market GTA 6 as a borderline PS5 exclusive, it turns out that Rockstar's magnum opus actually runs better on Xbox.

This is according to those tech wizards over at Digital Foundry, who have spent hours comparing the open world title across base PS5, PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S.

Now, we already know that GTA 6 isn't perfect on the standard PS5. It suffers from minor but sometimes prolonged frame rate drops during busy scenes — whether you're speeding through heavy traffic or fighting for your life in a particularly explosive combat encounter.

But in a rather shocking twist, the Xbox Series X outdoes the PS5 in this department. While Digital Foundry's testing shows that the frame rate dips are still present on the Series X, they're nowhere near as frequent.

They write: "PS5 suffers substantially more frequent frame rate drops than Series X, which is compounded by the fact that the Xbox machine also benefits from 120Hz VRR support to smooth out minor dips."

The article continues: "Ultimately, Series X is meaningfully better off."

This isn't what you'd expect, given that every PlayStation-related GTA 6 advertisement and trailer has boasted that the game 'Plays Best on PS5'.

Okay, so that slogan might technically be true if we're counting the PS5 Pro, where GTA 6 does perform best by some distance, thanks to a combination of the console's PSSR upscaler and increased GPU power.

But on base hardware, it's Microsoft that wins out.

#3825. Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - founded by ex-GTA veteran - has a mountain of debt, and the main plan for paying it back is litigation

"A coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary."

Beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the company created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt. And a huge chunk of that appears to be owed to Chinese gaming company NetEase (£36.5m), though more than £1m appears to be owed to Benzies himself.

This came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back. And the company's "largest" potential asset, according to the administrators, is litigation.

"Prior to the Company's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary.

"The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that any such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions."

This tallies with the narrative spun by co-company leader Mark Gerhard as the company waded into deep water. Gerhard blamed "organised espionage and corporate sabotage" for the studio's difficulties as multiple rounds of layoffs shredded Build a Rocket Boy. "People had their hands on the scale and deliberately tried to shape a negative narrative around the product," Gerhard said.

The situation he's referring to is likely the alleged smear campaign made against the game, which Gerhand reportedly claimed in an internal meeting this year was paid for by a "big American company" and then run by a UK company called Ritual Network, which apparently had influencers, journalists and staff at Build a Rocket Boy deliberately sabotage the game's release. That's according to an account of a videoed internal meeting reportedly seen by Insider Gaming earlier this year.

It had nothing to do with the dire state of Mindseye when it launched, then. Eurogamer awarded it one out of five stars, chastising its "ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat" in our Mindseye review.

Build a Rocket Boy was founded in 2016, and its first game, Everywhere - a sort of online gaming platform - was announced in 2022. It never materialised, but a part of that vision was carved out to become a standalone game experience of its own along the way, and that's how we got Mindseye - a take on a Grand Theft Auto formula. Whether or not the litigation is successful and can recoup any of Build a Rocket Boy's debts remains to be seen, but there's a financial mountain for the studio to climb if it hopes to operate again.

#3824. Rockstar has "been an awesome partner" for the Max Payne 1 and 2 remakes, says Remedy CEO

The companies are old friends in the industry

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Remakes of the first two Max Payne games are on the way, and Rockstar's been helping Remedy get the releases in order. According to the Control and Alan Wake studio, collaborating with the purveyor of GTA 6 has been absolutely grand so far.

Jean-Charles Gaudechon, the CEO of Remedy, described the working relationship between the two outfits in glowing terms for Game File. "Honestly, it's been great," he says. "You know why? Because I think they're super respectful of Remedy."

Respect is a good start to any collaboration. Gaudechon then doubles down, just to make it clear everything's positive right now. "I'll say it out loud: They've honestly been an awesome partner," he adds. "And it's no bullshit."

Well, it seems he doesn't have any complaints, anyway. Remedy and Rockstar actually have quite a bit of history, since the studio that gave us GTA actually worked on ports of the first Max Payne, then published the second outright.

It only makes sense, then, that they'd team back up to give both games a lick of paint and update them for modern hardware. As you may well be aware, it's been a while since Rockstar's done anything outside of the Grand Theft Auto or Red Dead Redemption mines.

Time was the developer and publisher would be involved in all sorts of projects, but nowadays the focus tends to be a little more streamlined. I guess that's what happens when you make the biggest games in the industry.

The two have been working on these do-overs since around 2022, and we don't have a release window yet. Perhaps now that Alan Wake 2 and Control: Resonant are out of the way, Remedy can put in more resource, while Rockstar can finally do something that isn't GTA 6. I mean, how much is there to do post-launch for such a game? Our boy Max is waiting, people – come on.

#3823. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

For what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

Indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.

If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

#3822. Infinity Nikki fans threaten to boycott game after promotion by Elon Musk's mother, but there may be a genuine reason for her involvement

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, cozy, open-world dress-up game, is at the centre of controversy again, though this time not because fans disliked one of the game's updates. Instead, it's because of… Elon Musk's mother.

Some Infinity Nikki fans are planning to boycott the game following the release of the game's latest trailer, which is narrated by Maye Musk. The trailer is for a new update - dubbed Cicia - which adds the ability to drive futuristic hovering cars. The reveal comes days after a widely mocked demonstration of Musk's own Tesla "flying car", which doesn't actually fly.

While some fans are worried Tesla's cars may be coming to the game, many also simply don't want their game associated with Elon Musk and his family.

"If they promote Tesla or mention him in the game I'm 100 percent dropping it," wrote one Reddit user (via The Gamer). "Why would they involve that man in a girly fashion game, and if they wanted a car brand partnership why not a Chinese one??!? Infold is addicted to negative attention I swear."

"If Tesla is somehow involved in the design of the car (or worse, an in-game promotion), then I might have to let go," wrote another person in the same thread. "Please please please be wrong."

Though Maye Musk's involvement might seem random, there may be a good explanation for it. "Here's something that might surprise people who only know her as Elon's mother: Maye Musk is a celebrity in China in her own right," Reddit user BarbieSpeedRacer explained.

"She's a successful model, an author, and a recognisable advertising personality. Her memoir became popular with Chinese readers, and she's appeared in campaigns and promotional events for brands including OPPO, Fila, and JNBY."

Her image as "a woman in her seventies who continues to work as a fashion model" is one that resonates with the game's Chinese audience, apparently, especially "among women interested in fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content".

"A Chinese company makes an advertisement featuring a celebrity popular in China, and an international fandom interprets that decision almost exclusively through the lens of American domestic politics," the post added.

So far, calls for a boycott don't appear to have coalesced into a movement, at least judging by the game's subreddit. Even if Western players were to organise one, it's not likely to hurt Infinity Nikki much, as most of the game's revenue - estimated at more than 80 percent - comes from Chinese players.

In Eurogamer's Infinity Nikki review, Jessica Orr said it advances the genre of open-world gacha games and brings competition to rival developer miHoYo, writing: "The changes in length, combat and progression all feel utterly invigorating compared to other Genshin-likes, and it's why Infinity Nikki feels like it could (and should) be on the same trajectory to shake up the gacha scene just like Genshin Impact did in 2020."

As well as giving a spit-and-polish digital release to various Warhammer classics, antique D&D games, and the cult ellipsoid horror games in the Ecstatica series, SNEG has been bug-fixing a bunch of strategy games from years gone by and getting them up on Steam and GOG. The latest trio to appear on digital platforms are Theocracy, Soldiers at War, and Warlords 4: Heroes of Etheria.

Warlords 4 was the final turn-based game in the beloved series, with the RTS spin-off series Warlords Battlecry already two games deep by the time of its release in 2003. This updated version supports resolutions up to 4K, and incorporates community fixes and a community-made campaign. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Soldiers at War took the X-COM/UFO turn-based tactics formula—this was 1998, X-COM still had a hyphen—and applied it to World War II. You'd choose a squad of eight from your platoon of 32 each mission, fighting through a campaign that started in North Africa and ended in Germany, gaining experience along the way. SNEG's version supports 1280x720 widescreen resolution. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Theocracy narrowly beat Total War to the punch in March of 2000 with its mix of turn-based civilization management and real-time battles, tasking you with uniting Aztec tribes before the prophesied Spanish invasion. You're on the clock with 100 years to use diplomacy, trade, and warfare to bring together an empire that can stand the test of time. The updated version still has a resolution of 800x600, but uses FSR 1 to scale up for modern displays. You'll be shocked to learn, it's also available on Steam and GOG.

All three games are designed to be easy to run on modern Windows systems, and have cloud saves and achievements. I'm tempted by Warlords 4, which I didn't play at the time because I'd moved over to the real-time Battlecry games by then. But I've still got fond memories of Warlords 2 Deluxe, which had 60 different worlds so if you were tired of raising griffon armies in its generic fantasy land you could conquer something oddball like Dante's Inferno instead. Or even make your own, right down to pixel-crafting the unit art. Good times.

#3820. Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

You lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

The game's New York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

Back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's New York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

#3819. Sony Will Support The Witcher 4's Marketing, Much Like GTA 6

The Witcher 4 dev CDPR has signed a marketing arrangement with Sony, which will likely see the latter promote the upcoming RPG similarly to GTA 6.

PlayStation pushed Rockstar’s latest release ridiculously hard, claiming it ‘Plays Best on PS5’.

While that may only actually apply to the PS5 Pro version, the Japanese giant could argue that its base hardware – which drops a few more frames than the Xbox Series X – still has the advantage of deeper DualSense integration et al.

Irrespective of slogan, CDPR’s CFO Piotr Nielubowicz told investors today that his company recently signed a new arrangement with Sony, which includes “the presence of our games on PlayStation and in PS Plus subscriptions, as well as our collaboration during the upcoming The Witcher 4 marketing campaign”.

Nielubowicz didn’t clarify whether this will be an exclusive marketing arrangement, but fans with good memories may recall the first footage of The Witcher 4 was presented on PS5.

With Microsoft owning a chunk of the Western RPG development scene, this seems like a shrewd move by Sony to me.

It’ll want to present CDPR’s next title as a major PlayStation title, because there’s still a possibility the next Elder Scrolls may skip its system entirely. (Although Xbox isn’t currently saying either way.)

Obviously we’ll need to wait and see how deep this partnership runs, but if it’s anything like Sony’s GTA 6 campaign, then it’ll be very aggressive to say the least.

#3818. You cannot replay missions in GTA 6, but you can use multiple save files, as Rockstar explains how it made missions "harder to fail"

You cannot replay GTA 6 missions again once you've completed them. This might be a shock to some people, since the option to do so was included in Rockstar games as recently as GTA 5, but here once you've made progress in the story, that's it. Our reviewer confirmed this in his 100+ hour playthrough of the title.

You can, of course, use the game's 15 save slots instead - but considering that there will be many, many more missions than there are slots, you're going to have to think about when and where you want to make a record of your progress. By my maths, that means you're going to want to make a new manual save for every 6.6 percent of the game you complete. There is, of course, an auto-save slot, too, that should help you out if you get Busted or Wasted. There will also be key story missions - you will be able to tell when they are, much like you could tell when there was about to be a big heist in GTA 5, a showdown in GTA: San Andreas, or a raid on a gang lord's mansion in GTA: Vice City - that you may want to save before attempting.

It seems, though, that it's going to be a bit harder than in previous games to hit that fail state in GTA 6. "The team embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project," says David Hynd, vice president of technology on GTA 6. "For example, we really wanted to reduce the number of Mission fails for the player experimenting or trying something different. And we wanted to encourage the player to do what felt right to them for their particular play style."

That means that Rockstar, by considering its deployment of standard gameplay mechanics and enemy AI, and re-evaluating how it approached mission and level design, has created "many different ways" for you to approach any given mission in the game. The result? "It's a lot harder to keep Missions as open as possible (especially in a game as large as this), but the freedom and flexibility it allows the player was worth it," says Hynd. He also notes that the team expects players to "learn and reapply" consistent rules in terms of how the world works - and be surprised when they do and don't apply.

In the previous game, you could access any previous mission you'd completed and be able to play it again on a whim. For GTA 5, you'd simply boot up Story Mode, open the pause menu, go to Game > Replay Mission, and pick the mission you want to play. GTA 6's structure is more complicated, though, hence why Rockstar made the decision to make progress this linear.

GTA 6 comes out tomorrow. You can find a breakdown of all the global launch times for GTA 6 at the link, and read our 5-star review of the game here. If you want to, ahem, 'travel to New Zealand' to get ahead of the timezones, it seems the country would be happy to have you.

#3816. Just how detailed is the audio in GTA 6? Well, even convenience store refrigerators "all have their own unique sounds", says Rockstar dev

If you've been online at all today, you'll know that what feels like the entire world is currently fawning over GTA 6. As the reviews dropped, one thing quickly became very clear: this is a game absolutely packed with detail. Our own Chris noted that, thanks to this focus on specific detail and unbelievable nuance, Grand Theft Auto 6 is "the most unbelievable video game world ever made". And it's no accident: this is something Rockstar put a lot of dedicated effort into.

It's been well-established that the studio has gone above and beyond to make this interactive world one of the most richly-developed we've ever seen: Rockstar has told us it "re-engineered" its weather systems to "achieve a sense of scale we haven't felt before," adding hurricanes, rainbows and heavy rain. It simulated and built a complex drug system, allowing Lucia and Jason to partake in drug use "directly from their inventory" and "at any time". But there are still details emerging from the dev team that are blowing my mind. And the most recent byte of information I saw was related to how Rockstar worked with sound.

"Much of the dynamic soundscape is informed by the incredibly detailed art throughout the world," explains Alastair MacGregor, vice president of audio at Rockstar. "One small example is that convenience store refrigerators all have their own unique sounds. In a run-down store, the refrigerators and freezers are loud and sound like they are badly maintained. Their compressor units can be heard mechanically whirring away from years of neglect. As a result, the bottles behind the doors can be heard shaking and the units click on and off more frequently. In an up-market store, the refrigerators are quieter, adding a subtle hum to the environment."

This level of detail is, quite frankly, absurd. It's a testament to granularity Rockstar is willing to go to in making Leonida feel truly lived-in and realistic. And this level of production isn't restricted to internal locations, either. "On the ambient side, we love the contrast between the manicured luxury islands, with the sizzle of crickets and lawn sprinklers backed by birdsong, yacht halyards clanging in the distance, and yard work going on, versus urban areas with the sounds of people living on top of each other - snatches of every genre of music, distant voices, cars peeling out, construction, the omnipresent hum of elderly air conditioners struggling with the humidity," continues MacGregor.

He goes on to say that if you're wandering the streets of Gellhorn - a coastal city in Kelly County on the western side of Leonida - it's acoustically a very different vibe than the high-rise centre of Vice City, where the sound bounces between the buildings. This means that the engine is handling not just the sounds of things as minute as bugs in the grass, but also how that sound travels, and interacts with other physical entities in the world. "We've spent years iterating on reverb technology to make sure that you can feel that - from the pops of cars backfiring to the wash of a helicopter passing by overhead to birds squawking in the trees," concludes MacGregor.

GTA 6 launches tomorrow - Thursday, 19th November - for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It's also worth noting that Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week.

#3815. Fish with a sniper rifle takes aim at Tim Sweeney's hopes and dreams, as genAI-free meme game tops Epic Games' vibe-coding megajam

Epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going big on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed company announced the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

The game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

"I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura."

Other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was announced that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

Still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide shows up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. Then again, he's been very busy posting important things about the situation with Jensen Huang and Nvidia lately, so maybe he hasn't noticed.

Yes, the last post I've linked there is the Sweens giggling at an AI image of him, Huang, Johan Andersson, and John Carmack as the heads carved into Mount Rushmore that he himself asked Grok to generate. As you do.

While most videogames got out of the way of Grand Theft Auto 6, on the day of its release The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth's free online DLC Repentance+ released an update. It included an easter egg daily challenge called Crime Mode (the seed is V1CE BSMT) with references to GTA like a wanted rating, guns, cops, and cars. Well, driveable minecarts.

What should have been an easy PR win for publisher Nicalis quickly turned sour as players pointed out that the music in Crime Mode sure sounds AI-generated. "It has that 'tinniness' that something like Suno generated music has", user ShweetStuff noted before looking at the music files and finding that, yep, there was Suno metadata in the file comments. Yet there was no AI disclosure on the DLC's Steam page.

Players were not thrilled by this development. Steam user reviews on The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ dropped to Overwhelmingly Negative, with only 8% positive recent reviews. Players put the blame on Nicalis, who licence Binding of Isaac from its original creator Edmund McMillen. "Edmund please take back control of the game", one said.

"Woke up to a shit show," McMillen wrote on the hatesite formerly known as Twitter when he found out what had happened, "obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned."

As of the latest update, the AI-generated music is gone. "It's a little sad given Joey Kuras (game's sound designer) did some excellent sounds for Mewgenics", ShweetStuff wrote, "but I suppose this is the industry nowadays!"

#3813. Ubisoft lay off 166 more staff, this time at their Montreal and Quebec City studios, while mumbling about "current production priorities and business needs"

"Our production needs are changing," publishers claim

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the company.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

"Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft said in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

Ubisoft Montreal are currently working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

Ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

Meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

Avengers: Doomsday is packed with heroes and villains from the past quarter-century of Marvel movies. But there's one all-powerful figure who is quite clearly being held back – and it's got fans wondering what (if anything) he will have to do in the upcoming battle against Doctor Doom.

So, how do you solve a problem like Bob? The character, first introduced in Thunderbolts, is currently lying dormant and chilling at New Avengerz HQ after being twisted into Sentry, a Superman-like figure who can send people to The Void with but a mere thought. Can you really leave that on the table if you're going up against Doom?

Well, it's a discussion that has spilled over to Reddit, with audiences debating the ramifications of unleashing Bob onto the world.

"Sentry is obviously gonna be there as an absolute last resort since the Avengers probably don’t wanna risk the Void coming back until they have no other choice," one said.

Another added, "Doom is a master manipulator. Giving him access to the Sentry/Void is like a death invitation."

Others joke that Bob will simply be Bob for the entirety of Avengers: Doomsday, kicking his feet and doing the dishes while the rest of the team brings the fight to Doom. There's a suggestion, though, that any major deaths – including to Florence Pugh's Yelena – would turn Bob into the unstoppable Sentry once more, with no allies to help calm him down this time.

Personally, I think Bob is being held back just to continue the age-old question of 'Who would win in a fight?' Pitting Sentry against Doom too soon not only risks answering it, but risks making Bob's power level seem diminished when he could be saved instead of Avengers: Secret Wars.

Discover what happens next – and if Bob puts on the Sentry suit once more – in Avengers: Doomsday, out in the UK on December 16 and in the US on December 18.

#3810. GTA 6 breaks the all-time livestream viewer record hours before it's available to play for most of the world

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in New Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

#3809. Ignore that other game about crime that's out and burgle some ugly farmhouses in Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" with a 2000s Cartoon Network vibe

Is there something going on today? A lot of talk about committing crimes and the like, I just can't quite put my finger on why… Ah well, couldn't be important or interesting. What is interesting, however, is Keepsake County, a "midwestern stealth game" that has launched on this inauspicious day about stealing stuff from "hideous farmhouses in the middle of nowhere."

With the sarcastic intro out the way, I will address the elephant in the room: Vovly's Adventure: Reslimed is out today too. Fine, fine, yes I know GTA 6 is the game everyone's talking about, but Forward Instinct, the devs behind Keepsake County, seem well aware of that in their launch day post for the game: "Folks, thanks for your incredible patience. Keepsake County is finally OUT! And yes, it is deeply ironic that it wound up being today, of all days, that we got the green light to finally release, but here we are."

Keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

Gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today!
